title: Pigeons and doves

names.gloss: bronzewing dove; if it sings out alone, a stranger is coming or someone may have died

identification.basis: The dictionary has words for the crested pigeon, the bronzewing, a small grey dove, a ground pigeon, a brown pigeon, a green pigeon and the Torres Strait pigeon. Within 30 km of Karma Waters the Atlas records the squatter pigeon, peaceful dove, bar-shouldered dove, crested pigeon, diamond dove and common bronzewing.

summary: The pigeons are the birds that walk, and the dictionary names them by where they walk: **[munungkul](word:munungkul)** and **[munwingkul](word:munwingkul)** the 'ground pigeon', **[karunkurr](word:karunkurr)** the 'crested pigeon', **[kurungka](word:kurungka)** and **[juku-juku](word:juku-juku)** the bronzewing, **[kuludu](word:kuludu)** the 'small grey' dove, **[kujuway](word:kujuway)** the 'brown and green pigeon', **[bakamu](word:bakamu)** the 'green pigeon' and **[wabul](word:wabul)** the Torres Strait pigeon of the coast [ref:hershberger1982]. The bronzewing carries a warning: 'if the *jukujuku* sings out alone the people know that a stranger is coming or that someone may have died' [ref:hershberger1982]. Which ones live where differs from place to place: see each place. The inland ones all eat seed and all must drink, which was the hunter's handle: Roth's western pigeon-netters dug a little pool of clear water beside the creek and flipped a net over the birds that came to it in the late afternoon [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[karunkurr](word:karunkurr)** 'crested pigeon'. **[kurungka](word:kurungka)** 'bronze wing pigeon'; **[juku-juku](word:juku-juku)** and **[jukujuku](word:jukujuku)** 'bronzewing dove', with the note that 'if the *jukujuku* sings out alone the people know that a stranger is coming or that someone may have died'. **[kuludu](word:kuludu)** 'dove, small grey'. **[munungkul](word:munungkul)** 'ground pigeon' and **[munwingkul](word:munwingkul)** 'species of dove (ground pigeon)'. **[kujuway](word:kujuway)** 'brown and green pigeon'. **[bakamu](word:bakamu)** 'green pigeon'. **[wabul](word:wabul)** 'Torres Strait Island pigeon', the white pied imperial pigeon of the coast and islands [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The inland pigeons and doves
sections.body:
**Squatter pigeon** (*Geophaps scripta*), the ground pigeon of the flats. 'It measures approximately 30 cm in length, weighing between 190 g and 250 g. Adults are mainly a grey-brown, with distinctive black and white facial markings and a white stripe up each of its sides. Blue-grey skin around the eyes'; it squats and freezes before it flies, which is its name [ref:wiki-squatter]. The [woodland](entry:woodland) page has it walking the same seed ground as the finches.

**Peaceful dove** (*Geopelia placida*). 'A relatively small pigeon and varies in length from 19 to 21 centimetres. The peaceful dove has a pink-grey breast with chequered grey-brown wings. Thin striations of black appear around the neck'; 'calls of the peaceful dove are high-pitched "doodle-doo", "co-co-coo"'; 'breeding occurs ... from March to June in northern Australia. Nests are built on horizontal branches of trees. Two white eggs are laid' [ref:wiki-peaceful-dove].

**Bar-shouldered dove** (*G. humeralis*). 'A blue-grey breast with chequered brown-bronze wings', a copper nape; 'often found in pairs, groups or large loose flocks and are seen commonly feeding on the ground feeding on seeds. Flight is direct and swift and wings whistle while the birds are in flight'; 'usually found in thick vegetation where water is present, damp gullies ... mangroves ... swamps' [ref:wiki-bar-shouldered-dove].

**Crested pigeon** (*Ocyphaps lophotes*, *karunkurr*). '30 to 34 cm ... grey with tinges of brown, pink and green. It has a feathered, but slender, black spike on top of the head. It runs with the crest erect'; 'if startled, the crested pigeon takes to the air with a distinctive whistling', the sound of air over a modified wing feather; 'found in lightly wooded grasslands', at watercourses and homesteads, and 'their habitat has expanded rapidly since settlement' [ref:wiki-crested-pigeon].

**Common bronzewing** (*Phaps chalcoptera*, *kurungka*). 'A medium-sized, heavily built pigeon', 'between 30 and 36 centimetres in length', with the bronze wing patch; 'rarely found far from a source of water, common bronzewings either travel alone or in pairs or in flocks, and are usually cautious, making approach by humans or other animals difficult'; 'since the pigeon must drink frequently, it utilizes watering holes'; it nests low in a bush and both parents feed the young on crop milk [ref:wiki-bronzewing].

**Diamond dove** (*G. cuneata*). The tiny dove of the dry country, 'weighing only about 35 g', with white spots on the wings and a red eye-ring; 'often seen on the ground, where it runs with a waddling gait'; 'the wings can make a whistling "frrr" noise when flying'; it feeds 'off seed mostly from grasses' near water [ref:wiki-diamond-dove].

**Roth's pigeon hunting, 1901.** In the west the flock pigeons, 'where they can be met with in thousands, are caught in small-mesh nets of a particular shape. The upper edge of this net is attached along its whole length to a long thin curved stick, the handle of which is free, and held by the hunter ... its lower edge, about 10 feet or 12 feet in length ... fixed along its entire extent into the ground by means of little forked twigs. A small artificial water-hole, about 6 feet long and 2 feet or 3 feet wide, is made parallel with, and at a little distance from, the main channel where the birds have been noticed to usually alight; this miniature lake is effected by a scooping up with the hands, and, what with the sandy formation of the soil, it quickly fills with beautiful clear water. When in the late afternoon the birds come down to drink, they will in all probability make for it, thinking it to be a new hole and its water fresher. The hunter knows this, and lays his net quite flat upon the ground ... he hides himself in a crouching position under some bushes and sand close enough to have full control of the long handle. The pigeons settle down in time, walk on and over the net, and collect on the miniature lake, where they "sit" the water like ducks. As soon as the individual in ambush thinks the opportunity suitable, he revolves the net around its fixed axis by a very swift movement of the arm and wrist, thus enclosing the unsuspecting birds beneath'. A smaller version at Cloncurry took galahs and other birds at a hole 'usually anywhere in the open ... especially in the summer months when all the natural water-channels have dried up'; on the Georgina a hook-boomerang was thrown into the flock [ref:roth1901]. On the Tully coast the Torres Strait pigeons were knocked out of their low evening flight home to the islands with a thrown stick, 'as many as four birds on occasion with the one throw', or struck from a tree-top with a fifteen-foot switch, the hunter tied to the tree by a cane round his waist [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Telling them
sections.body:
- **Squatter pigeon**: a plump grey-brown pigeon with a black-and-white face, on the ground, freezing then exploding into flight [ref:wiki-squatter].
- **Peaceful dove**: small, barred neck, blue eye-ring, 'doodle-doo' [ref:wiki-peaceful-dove].
- **Bar-shouldered dove**: bigger, a copper nape, in the damp scrub, 'cook-a-wook' [ref:wiki-bar-shouldered-dove].
- **Crested pigeon**: the spike on the head, the whistling take-off [ref:wiki-crested-pigeon].
- **Bronzewing**: heavy, a bronze flash on the wing, a pale forehead on the male, wary [ref:wiki-bronzewing].
- **Diamond dove**: tiny, white-spotted, a red eye-ring [ref:wiki-diamond-dove].
- **Torres Strait pigeon** (*wabul*): big, white with black wingtips, the pigeon of the coast and islands [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **A whistle of wings** from the ground: a crested pigeon or a bronzewing going up [ref:wiki-crested-pigeon] [ref:wiki-bronzewing].
- **Birds walking in to water at evening** along the same line each day: the pigeons' drinking time, Roth's time [ref:roth1901].
- **Two white eggs on a few sticks** on a branch, from March to June [ref:wiki-peaceful-dove].
- **A bronzewing calling alone**: the dictionary's warning [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Seed-husk scratchings** under the grass seed-heads: the flock has fed [ref:wiki-squatter].

sections.heading: Where they are
sections.body: The squatter pigeon and the diamond dove on the open grassy [woodland](entry:woodland) and the flats; the peaceful dove everywhere; the bar-shouldered dove in the damp scrub of the river; the crested pigeon at the dams and the homestead; the bronzewing in any cover near water [ref:wiki-squatter] [ref:wiki-diamond-dove] [ref:wiki-bar-shouldered-dove] [ref:wiki-crested-pigeon] [ref:wiki-bronzewing] [ref:re-woodland]. All of them at the water's edge in the late afternoon.

sections.heading: The seed birds and the water
sections.body: The pigeons turn the [grass](entry:blady-grass) seed of the flats into meat, and the daily walk to water is the thing that made them catchable and makes them hawk food: the [goshawk](entry:eagles-and-hawks) 'often hunt[s] near farmland or wetlands, where birds such as ducks, cockatoos and pigeons' gather, and the [pythons](entry:pythons) and [goannas](entry:goanna) take the flimsy nests [ref:wiki-brown-goshawk] [ref:wiki-peaceful-dove]. The squatter pigeon's southern form has declined with grazing and the loss of seeding grass [ref:wiki-squatter].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: The doves breed from March to June in the north, after the wet when the grass has seeded; the pigeons concentrate at the last water in the late dry, which was the western netters' season, 'especially in the summer months when all the natural water-channels have dried up' [ref:wiki-peaceful-dove] [ref:roth1901]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Meat**: netted at the made water-hole, or knocked down from the evening flight [ref:roth1901].
- **Eggs and squabs** from the nests: see each place.
- **A warning**: the bronzewing calling alone [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The flip-net at the water
sections.body:
From Roth's western account, which works on any pigeon that walks to water [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Watch where the birds come to drink** in the late afternoon, and which side they land on.
2. **Scoop a little pool** in the sand beside the creek, a couple of metres long, which fills clear from below; the birds take it for fresher water [ref:roth1901].
3. **Make the net**: fine mesh, the top edge tied along a long curved stick with a free handle, the bottom edge longer than the top and pegged to the ground with forked twigs along the far side of the pool [ref:roth1901].
4. **Lay the net flat** on the ground, hide crouched under bushes and sand within reach of the handle [ref:roth1901].
5. **When the birds have walked over the net and settled on the water**, flip the net over on its pegged edge with 'a very swift movement of the arm and wrist' [ref:roth1901].
6. **Pluck and cook** on the coals; a pigeon is a mouthful each.
7. **Leave the nesting birds** from March to June [ref:wiki-peaceful-dove].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Native birds are protected wildlife in Queensland under the *Nature Conservation Act 1992*; native title holders hunting for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs are covered by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* [ref:qld-nca] [ref:alrc].
- The water-hole where the pigeons drink is where the [snakes](entry:snakes) and the crocodile wait too [ref:crocwise].
- The dictionary's bronzewing warning is a thing to know, not a thing to fear [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Matching the dictionary's nine pigeon words to the species is a job for Kuku Yalanji speakers; the contribution box below is for that [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: Pigeons and doves are among the commonest birds of the Hann River country. The Atlas of Living Australia holds 3,516 records of the pigeon family, from 1896 to 2026, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru; most are the **bar-shouldered dove** and the **peaceful dove** [ref:ala-hann-pigeons]. No published record says how the Possum, Thaypan or Lama Lama peoples hunted them; the methods in the general sections come from other districts.

sections.heading: Names in Kuku Thaypan
sections.body: The Hann's own languages are not Kuku Yalanji. In Kuku Thaypan the Hunter-Gatherer Language Database records **aperrawng** for the crested pigeon, with the linguist's note 'uncertain segmentation', and **athuku-athuku** for the peaceful dove, a doubled-up word like the Kuku Yalanji *juku-juku* [ref:hgdb-thaypan] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Which ones are here
sections.body:
In the Atlas box around the middle Hann [ref:ala-hann-pigeons]:

- **Bar-shouldered dove**: 1,431 records, 1964–2026.
- **Peaceful dove**: 1,342 records, 1972–2025.
- **Common bronzewing**: 208 records, 1976–2025.
- **Diamond dove**: 202 records, 1963–2025.
- **Squatter pigeon**: 164 records, 1982–2025.
- **Torresian imperial pigeon** (*Ducula spilorrhoa*): 128 records, 1987–2024.
- **Crested pigeon**: only 7 records, 1998–2025.

The Torresian imperial pigeon is also called the 'Torres Strait pigeon', the same English name the dictionary gives for [wabul](word:wabul). It feeds 'almost exclusively on fruit', not seed [ref:wiki-torresian] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Their year here
sections.body: The seed doves must drink every day. Here the last water is never far: the Hann has not stopped flowing on any day since its gauge began in 1968, even in the late dry when the plains are 'brown and parched' [ref:bom-105001b] [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The white imperial pigeons come and go: 'The population in Queensland leaves for New Guinea in February–April and returns in July–August' [ref:wiki-torresian].

sections.heading: How people used them here
sections.body: Nothing is published on pigeon hunting by the peoples of the Hann. Roth's pigeon nets are from the western rivers and his Torres Strait pigeon hunting is from the lower Tully [ref:roth1901]. The Possum People's evidence to the Federal Court names 'plain turkeys' among the birds hunted on the upper Hann, not pigeons [ref:fca-possum]. See the general sections.

locations.summary: On the Karma Waters flats the squatter pigeon, fifty-four records within 30 km, is the ground pigeon, 'mainly a grey-brown, with distinctive black and white facial markings and a white stripe up each of its sides'; the peaceful dove, forty-five, and the bar-shouldered dove, twenty-two, are the small doves of the river scrub; the crested pigeon, fourteen, whistles up from the dams; the diamond dove, nine, and the common bronzewing, five, come to the water [ref:ala-aves] [ref:wiki-squatter] [ref:wiki-peaceful-dove] [ref:wiki-bar-shouldered-dove] [ref:wiki-crested-pigeon] [ref:wiki-diamond-dove] [ref:wiki-bronzewing].

sections.heading: Grass and fire here
sections.body: The northern squatter pigeons here depend on the grass being burnt cool and left to seed [ref:wiki-squatter] [ref:re-woodland].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The squatter pigeons and peaceful doves walk the Karma Waters tracks ahead of every vehicle, and the crested pigeons whistle up from every dam [ref:ala-aves]. Native title holders' hunting rights under section 211 are recognised in the Western Yalanji determinations [ref:wyac2020].

locations.summary: The dictionary's pigeon words were recorded on the Eastern Kuku Yalanji coast, and some of them are coast and rainforest birds: **[kujuway](word:kujuway)** the 'brown and green pigeon', **[bakamu](word:bakamu)** the 'green pigeon' and **[wabul](word:wabul)** the 'Torres Strait Island pigeon' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: How people used them here
sections.body:
- **Eggs and squabs**: Roth's rule for the whole eastern coast of North Queensland was that 'with the smaller birds, it is the eggs and fledgelings which are rather sought for' [ref:roth1901].
- **Feathers** on the children's target wheel, among the Bloomfield Kuku Yalanji [ref:anderson1996].
